group.passage:
In the early nineteenth century, carrying a living plant across an ocean was close to hopeless. Collectors packed young plants into boxes, loaded them onto ships, and hoped for the best, but few survived months at sea. In 1819 an East India Company surgeon in Macao estimated that only one plant in a thousand sent from China to London arrived alive.
The answer was found by accident. In 1829 Nathaniel Ward, a London doctor, buried the chrysalis of a moth in damp soil inside a glass bottle and closed the lid. The moth never came out, but a fern and some grass soon sprouted. Ward's own garden had done poorly, since the polluted air of east London poisoned his plants. Sealed off from that air, the seedlings in the bottle stayed healthy for years without being watered. Water given off by their leaves gathered on the glass and ran back down into the soil, where the roots could use it again.
Ward then tested the idea at sea. In 1833 he packed ferns and grasses into two glass-sided wooden cases and shipped them to Sydney, where almost all of the plants arrived alive. The cases were refilled with Australian plants for the trip home, a voyage of about eight months through temperatures from above 30°C to below freezing. Those plants, too, reached London in good health. In 1842 Ward described his method in a book, and his boxes became known as Wardian cases.
For roughly the next hundred years, nurseries and botanical gardens moved plants around the world in them; one nursery alone sent out more than 500. Tea, rubber, and bananas all crossed oceans this way. In many Victorian homes, glass cases full of ferns became fashionable, the ancestors of today's terrariums.
Yet the cases also held soil, and the soil was rarely empty. Insects, worms, and unwanted seeds traveled too, and many reached their new homes alive. In 1862 an American doctor returning from Japan brought Japanese honeysuckle home in Wardian cases; the vine later spread through woodlands across the eastern United States. In 1924 a senior US agriculture official warned that the cases had probably spread more harmful pests than almost any other carrier. Stricter rules followed. By the 1940s the cases had largely fallen out of use, and in the 1960s the last of them gave way to plastic bags and air freight, which let plants travel quickly and without soil.

translation_zh.text:
十九世紀初，要讓一株活的植物橫渡海洋，幾乎是不可能的事。採集者把幼苗裝進箱子、搬上船，然後聽天由命，但在海上航行好幾個月之後，很少有植物能活下來。1819 年，一位駐澳門的東印度公司外科醫生估計，從中國運往倫敦的植物，一千株只有一株能活著抵達。
解決的辦法是意外發現的。1829 年，倫敦醫生納撒尼爾・沃德把一個蛾蛹埋在玻璃瓶裡的濕土中，然後蓋上蓋子。蛾始終沒有破蛹而出，土裡卻很快冒出了一株蕨類和一些青草。沃德自家的花園一向種不好，因為倫敦東區受污染的空氣毒害了他的植物。瓶中的幼苗和那樣的空氣隔絕，結果好幾年不用澆水，依然長得很健康。葉子散發出的水分凝結在玻璃上，再流回土裡，讓根部可以重複利用。
接著，沃德把這個構想拿到海上測試。1833 年，他把蕨類和青草裝進兩個玻璃側板的木箱，用船運往雪梨，結果幾乎所有植物都活著抵達。箱子隨後重新裝進澳洲的植物，準備運回英國；這趟航程約八個月，溫度從 30°C 以上到冰點以下，但這些植物同樣健健康康地抵達倫敦。1842 年，沃德在一本書中說明了他的方法，他的箱子也被稱為「沃德箱」。
在大約一百年間，苗圃和植物園用沃德箱把植物運往世界各地；光是一家苗圃就送出了五百多個。茶樹、橡膠樹和香蕉都是這樣漂洋過海的。在許多維多利亞時代的家庭裡，裝滿蕨類的玻璃箱成了時髦的擺設，也就是今天玻璃生態瓶的前身。
然而，箱子裡也裝著土壤，而土壤裡很少是空無一物的。昆蟲、蟲子和不請自來的種子也一起上路，而且很多活著抵達了新的地方。1862 年，一位從日本返國的美國醫生用沃德箱帶回日本忍冬；這種藤蔓後來蔓延到美國東部各地的林地。1924 年，一位美國農業部的高階官員警告，沃德箱散播的有害生物，可能比其他幾乎任何載具都多。之後相關規定變得更嚴格。到了 1940 年代，沃德箱大致上已不再使用；1960 年代，最後一批也被塑膠袋和空運取代——這兩者讓植物能夠快速運送，而且不必帶土。

open_tasks.prompt: Today many countries limit how plants and soil can be brought across their borders. Do you think such rules are necessary? Answer in 1–2 English sentences and use an example from the passage.
reference_answers: Yes, because soil can carry insects and seeds that harm local nature, just as Japanese honeysuckle spread through American woodlands after it arrived in Wardian cases.
I think they are necessary, since the Wardian case showed that moving plants also moves pests, and once a plant like Japanese honeysuckle escapes, it is very hard to stop.

In 1833 Ward shipped ferns and grasses in two glass-sided wooden cases to Sydney, where almost all of the plants arrived alive.（f7；Arnold Arboretum 2021 原頁：two sealed glass cases planted with ferns, grasses, and mosses…all but three of the plants still alive；Arnoldia 稱沃德箱 a simple case made of wood and glass）

The cases were refilled with Australian plants; the voyage home took about eight months through temperatures from above 30°C to below freezing, and the plants arrived healthy.（f8；Arnoldia：over 30°C…to -7°C near Cape Horn；eight months later）
In 1842 Ward described his method in a book, and the boxes became known as Wardian cases.（f9；Arnoldia、Courtauld：On the Growth of Plants in Closely Glazed Cases, 1842）

For roughly the next hundred years nurseries and botanical gardens moved plants in them; one nursery sent out more than 500.（f10、f18；Arnoldia：a prime mover for botanical enterprises for over a century；Loddiges put into circulation over five hundred cases）
Tea, rubber and bananas crossed oceans this way.（f11；Arnoldia：tea plants from China to India、rubber via Kew、dwarf Cavendish banana）
Fern cases became fashionable in Victorian homes, ancestors of today's terrariums.（f12；Courtauld：Victorian fern craze；Arnoldia：We would call this system a terrarium today）
The cases held soil; insects, worms and unwanted seeds traveled too.（f13、f15；Arboretum 2021：plants invariably arrived with insects and pathogens…stowaway seeds germinated；Galloway 的 nematodes）

In 1862 an American doctor returning from Japan brought Japanese honeysuckle in Wardian cases; it later spread through woodlands across the eastern United States.（f14；Arnoldia：Hall returned from Japan with six more Wardian cases…Japanese honeysuckle…invaded woodlands across the eastern United States）

In 1924 a senior US agriculture official warned the cases had probably spread more harmful pests than almost any other carrier.（f15；Arnoldia：Galloway…scattering more dangerous insects, nematodes, and other pests）

Stricter rules followed; by the 1940s the cases were largely out of use, and in the 1960s the last gave way to plastic bags and air freight that let plants travel without soil.（f16、f17；Arnoldia：by the 1940s it was largely phased out…last journeys…in the 1960s…polyethylene bags and…air transport；Arboretum 2021：plant quarantines…moved without soil, wrapped in plastic）
